name: cover-subtitle
text: Build a message that can find and fix its own one-bit mistake.
textPreview: Build a message that can find and fix its own one-bit mistake.

alt: Seven binary tiles travel through three scanning beams; one tile is visibly corrupted

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Welcome students as returning signal engineers. Ask them to silently count the seven tiles and spot the corrupted one. Say: Today the challenge is not merely to notice damage; it is to make the message tell us exactly where the damage happened. Do not name Hamming codes yet.


[Sources]
- Hero illustration generated for this deck with OpenAI ImageGen on 2026-08-25; no external asset.
- Session theme continues the local GLITCH! math-circle deck in this workspace.
[/Sources]

name: title-2
text: Your mission has one precise finish line
textPreview: Your mission has one precise finish line

name: text
text: By the end, you will be able to…
textPreview: By the end, you will be able to…

name: text
text: You will invent every ingredient along the way.
textPreview: You will invent every ingredient along the way.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Read the three verbs aloud. Students give a thumbs-sideways or thumbs-up for how possible this feels. Tell them the solo challenge is open-note and the worksheet is their lab notebook.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-3
text: A damaged message cannot explain itself
textPreview: A damaged message cannot explain itself

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Give 30 seconds of silence, then pairs discuss. Accept both 0 and 1 as possible. Key conclusion: without extra structure, the receiver cannot know. Ask: What extra information could we add without sending the whole message twice? Worksheet 1A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-4
text: One extra bit can make a promise
textPreview: One extra bit can make a promise

name: text
text: EVEN PARITY: the total number of 1s must be even.
textPreview: EVEN PARITY: the total number of 1s must be even.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Model 101. Then teams complete 111, 000, and 0101 on Worksheet 1B. Answers: 111 needs 1; 000 needs 0; 0101 needs 0. Ask teams to hold up fingers 0 or 1 together. Emphasize the convention is even parity.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-5
text: Parity raises an alarm—but gives no address
textPreview: Parity raises an alarm—but gives no address

name: text
text: One check gives one yes/no answer. We need several overlapping checks.
textPreview: One check gives one yes/no answer. We need several overlapping checks.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Ask students to name all four possible single-bit changes that could create odd parity. Conclude that one alarm detects a problem but cannot locate it. This creates the need for overlapping checks.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-6
text: Three yes/no questions can name any position 1–7
textPreview: Three yes/no questions can name any position 1–7

name: text
text: Challenge: choose a secret position. Your partner asks only these three questions.
textPreview: Challenge: choose a secret position. Your partner asks only these three questions.

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Pairs play three rounds. Partner A chooses a position 1–7; Partner B asks the three displayed questions and records yes/no. They should discover each position has a unique pattern. If stuck, suggest writing the three answers next to each number on Worksheet 1C. Do not introduce binary notation unless students mention it.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-7
text: The failed checks spell the position’s address
textPreview: The failed checks spell the position’s address

name: text
text: Example: position 6 answers NO, YES, YES → 2 + 4 = 6
textPreview: Example: position 6 answers NO, YES, YES → 2 + 4 = 6

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Have the room read down the column for position 6: check 1 no, check 2 yes, check 4 yes. The labels of the YES rows add to 6. Ask for the address of positions 3, 5, and 7. Answers: 1+2=3; 1+4=5; 1+2+4=7. Worksheet 1C.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Round 1: stand if check 1 covers you.
textPreview: Round 1: stand if check 1 covers you.

name: text
text: Round 2: stand if check 2 covers you.
textPreview: Round 2: stand if check 2 covers you.

name: text
text: Round 3: stand if check 4 covers you.
textPreview: Round 3: stand if check 4 covers you.

name: text
text: Finale: one person flips their bit. Which checks become odd?
textPreview: Finale: one person flips their bit. Which checks become odd?

text:
Timing: 7 minutes.

Invite seven volunteers and give each a position card 1–7. For each check, students in that group stand or raise a card. Then secretly tap one volunteer to flip their bit card. The class counts each check group and uses the labels of odd groups to name the volunteer. Rotate volunteers if time. This physicalizes the syndrome before any formal encoding.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-9
text: Powers of two become the check-bit stations
textPreview: Powers of two become the check-bit stations

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Name the positions and roles. Ask why 1, 2, and 4 are special: they are exactly the check labels and each belongs to only its own check group. Students fill the role row on Worksheet 2A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-10
text: Each check bit controls its own overlapping group
textPreview: Each check bit controls its own overlapping group

name: text
text: Your rule: choose each check bit so its whole row has an even number of 1s.
textPreview: Your rule: choose each check bit so its whole row has an even number of 1s.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Point out that each check includes its own check-bit position. Students trace the three sets on Worksheet 2A. Quick call-and-response: Does check 1 cover 6? no. Does check 2 cover 6? yes. Does check 4 cover 6? yes.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-11
text: Training wheels: use three message bits first
textPreview: Training wheels: use three message bits first

name: text
text: Place data in 3, 5, 6. Lock position 7 at zero.
textPreview: Place data in 3, 5, 6. Lock position 7 at zero.

name: text
text: This is a restricted practice version—not the standard Hamming(7,3) code.
textPreview: This is a restricted practice version—not the standard Hamming(7,3) code.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Explain the accuracy note briefly: we are taking the full seven-slot machine and simply fixing the last message slot at 0. That lets students practice all three parity checks with less cognitive load. Worksheet 2B.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Find p₁, p₂, p₄ so every check group is even.
textPreview: Find p₁, p₂, p₄ so every check group is even.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Pairs solve without a formula. Hint ladder: (1) start with check 1 positions 1,3,5,7; (2) count the known 1s; (3) choose p1 to make that count even; repeat for checks 2 and 4. Expected p1=1, p2=0, p4=1. Do not reveal until most pairs have committed.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

Timing: 2 minutes.

Have three students each verify one check aloud. Ask what would change if the original three bits were different: only the count in the groups, not the groups themselves.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-14
text: Now unlock position 7: this is Hamming(7,4)
textPreview: Now unlock position 7: this is Hamming(7,4)

name: text
text: The same three checks still do all the work.
textPreview: The same three checks still do all the work.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Reveal the notation: Hamming(7,4) means seven transmitted bits carry four message bits. The three check bits are the redundancy that buys single-error correction. Students circle the four data stations on Worksheet 3A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: step-body-0
text: Keep the address above every slot.
textPreview: Keep the address above every slot.

name: step-body-2
text: Choose p₁,p₂,p₄ so each group is even.
textPreview: Choose p₁,p₂,p₄ so each group is even.

name: step-body-3
text: Recount all three groups before sending.
textPreview: Recount all three groups before sending.

text:
Timing: 3 minutes.

Students write this recipe in their own words on Worksheet 3A. Stress that the order of p1, p2, p4 does not matter mathematically because each is in only its own check position, but a consistent order prevents mistakes.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: One partner sets the checks. The other partner audits all three groups.
textPreview: One partner sets the checks. The other partner audits all three groups.

text:
Timing: 7 minutes.

Pairs encode 1011. Hint ladder: p1 checks positions 1,3,5,7; p2 checks 2,3,6,7; p4 checks 4,5,6,7. Expected p1=0, p2=1, p4=0. Ask auditors to mark each check even before the reveal.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

Timing: 2 minutes.

Verify all three groups. Ask students to point to the original message bits in the codeword. This prepares later extraction after repair.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-18
text: Speed round: can your team encode without hints?
textPreview: Speed round: can your team encode without hints?

text:
Timing: 6 minutes.

Assign one message per teammate, then cross-audit. Answers: 0000→0000000; 1111→1111111; 0101→0100101; 1100→0111100. If a team finishes early, have them prove why 1111 maps to seven 1s.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: When you return: we make the message point to its own mistake.
textPreview: When you return: we make the message point to its own mistake.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Take a real five-minute break. Leave the slide projected. Resume by asking students to restate the encoding roles from memory.

name: title-20
text: A corrupted codeword makes specific checks fail
textPreview: A corrupted codeword makes specific checks fail

name: text
text: Run all three parity checks again.
textPreview: Run all three parity checks again.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Students recount each check group for received 0110001. Check 1 has two ones and passes; checks 2 and 4 each have three ones and fail. Ask: Which position belongs to check 2 and check 4 but not check 1? Worksheet 4A.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Flip bit 6, then verify all checks pass.
textPreview: Flip bit 6, then verify all checks pass.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Name this three-check result the syndrome. The most beginner-friendly rule is to add the labels of failed checks. Optionally connect to binary: fail pattern check4-check2-check1 is 110₂ = 6. Students correct position 6 from 0 back to 1 and recover 0110011.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-22
text: The syndrome is a seven-way pointer
textPreview: The syndrome is a seven-way pointer

name: text
text: No failed checks → address 0 → no error
textPreview: No failed checks → address 0 → no error

name: text
text: Any nonzero address 1–7 → flip that position
textPreview: Any nonzero address 1–7 → flip that position

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Connect back to the address detective game: an error at one position flips exactly the checks that cover that position, so the failed-check pattern is unique. Emphasize the one-error assumption.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-23
text: Repair first; read the message second
textPreview: Repair first; read the message second

name: step-body-0
text: Mark each group pass or fail.
textPreview: Mark each group pass or fail.

name: step-body-1
text: Add labels of the failed checks.
textPreview: Add labels of the failed checks.

name: step-body-2
text: Change the bit at that address.
textPreview: Change the bit at that address.

text:
Timing: 2 minutes.

Students copy the decode routine onto Worksheet 4A. Make them say the order aloud: checks, address, flip, extract. Warn that extracting before repairing can preserve the wrong data bit.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-24
text: Packet repair race: two corrupted transmissions
textPreview: Packet repair race: two corrupted transmissions

name: text
text: Every teammate must be able to explain one failed check.
textPreview: Every teammate must be able to explain one failed check.

text:
Timing: 7 minutes.

Teams repair both. Packet A 0101101 has only check 4 failing, so error position 4; corrected 0100101; message 0101. Packet B 0111101 has all checks failing, so error position 7; corrected 0111100; message 1100. Require visible check counts, not guesses.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: step-body-2
text: Flip exactly one position; record it secretly.
textPreview: Flip exactly one position; record it secretly.

name: step-body-3
text: Swap papers. Repair and recover the message.
textPreview: Swap papers. Repair and recover the message.

name: text
text: Success = corrected codeword + recovered message + explanation
textPreview: Success = corrected codeword + recovered message + explanation

text:
Timing: 12 minutes.

Use Worksheet 5A. First partner creates while the other audits, then both secretly flip one bit and swap. Receiver shows all checks and the syndrome. Sender verifies the recovered message. If a pair finishes, repeat with a check-bit error and compare with a data-bit error. This is the longest independent practice before the solo task.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-26
text: One-error correction has a sharp boundary
textPreview: One-error correction has a sharp boundary

name: text
text:
may imitate one error
do not trust the repair
textPreview: may imitate one error | do not trust the repair

name: text
text: Guarantee: Hamming(7,4) corrects any single-bit error—not every possible pattern of damage.
textPreview: Guarantee: Hamming(7,4) corrects any single-bit error—not every possible pattern of damage.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Have students predict what two errors might do, then state the guarantee precisely. A standard Hamming(7,4) decoder can miscorrect a double error because the two error addresses combine into a third nonzero syndrome. Avoid implying it reliably detects two errors.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: title-27
text: Bonus eighth bit: detect two errors
textPreview: Bonus eighth bit: detect two errors

name: text
text: → detect two errors; do not correct
textPreview: → detect two errors; do not correct

name: text
text: The extra bit turns single-error correction into SECDED: single-error correction, double-error detection.
textPreview: The extra bit turns single-error correction into SECDED: single-error correction, double-error detection.

text:
Timing: 4 minutes.

Treat this as optional enrichment, not required mastery. Ask students to add an eighth overall parity bit to 0110011: it contains four ones, so bit 8 is 0. Explain the four decoding cases only if time; Worksheet 6B contains the complete table.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: Show p₁, p₂, p₄ and audit all checks.
textPreview: Show p₁, p₂, p₄ and audit all checks.

name: text
text: Name the bad position and recover the message.
textPreview: Name the bad position and recover the message.

name: text
text: No partner. Notes allowed. Every check must be visible.
textPreview: No partner. Notes allowed. Every check must be visible.

text:
Timing: 5 minutes.

Students work alone. Part A expected codeword 0011001. Part B: checks 1 and 4 fail, so error position 5; correct to 0011001; extract 1001. Use this as the learning-outcome check. Provide only process prompts: roles, check sets, add failed labels.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: text
text: If your method found both answers, you can do Hamming(7,4).
textPreview: If your method found both answers, you can do Hamming(7,4).

text:
Timing: 1 minute.

Students self-check in a different color and fix any process error. Collect or glance at Part B to see who independently met the outcome. Do not frame corrections as failure; the visible method identifies exactly where the thinking diverged.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]

name: closing-title
text: You built a message that points to its own mistake.
textPreview: You built a message that points to its own mistake.

name: text
text: Exit whisper: What is the one step you are least likely to forget?
textPreview: Exit whisper: What is the one step you are least likely to forget?

text:
Timing: 1 minute.

Pairs share one memorable step. Close by naming Hamming's achievement: not magic, but three deliberately overlapping parity questions. Invite students to keep the worksheet as a reusable decoder guide.

[Sources]
- R. W. Hamming, “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes,” Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x
[/Sources]
